segments.text: What happens if you're stranded in the middle of the ocean, with absolutely nothing around you?
First comes the shock.
In cold water, your body gasps uncontrollably, and one gasp underwater can drown you.
You look around.
No boat. No land.
Just horizon, in every direction.
So you swim, toward nothing.
Exhaustion is one of the biggest killers out here,
and drowning is usually quiet. No splashing, no cries for help.
Instead, float.
Tilt your head back, ears under, arms and legs spread.
It buys you time.
Hours pass.
There's no shade, and the water bounces sunlight right back into your face.
Soon, you're desperately thirsty.
But seawater is about three and a half percent salt.
To flush it out, your kidneys need more water than you drank. Every sip leaves you more dehydrated.
And you're not alone.
Small fish shelter in your shadow.
Then, something bigger comes to look.
Bites are rare, but splashing draws attention, so you stay still.
Then the sun sets.
Even warm water is colder than your body, and it drains your heat far faster than air.
In cold seas, hypothermia can kill within hours.
The night is pitch black, except for plankton that glow every time you move.
By day two, thirst and exhaustion cloud your mind.
Some survivors have seen ships and land that weren't there.
Without fresh water, you have days, not weeks.
But people do survive. In 2022, a man who fell from a cruise ship lasted at least fifteen hours in the Gulf of Mexico, with no life jacket.
So what kills you out here?
In cold water, shock and hypothermia.
In warm water, exhaustion, drowning, and thirst.
Your odds depend on the water temperature, staying afloat, and whether anyone knows you're missing.
Because out here, survival isn't about swimming to safety.
It's about lasting long enough to be found.
